I like eating a variety of different categories, so whenever I get the chance, I eat creamy tonkotsu, but maybe it's because it's gone out of style, but there aren't as many tonkotsu ramen restaurants that taste like that.
Among them, we visited Ban Lai, which is famous and has Cheongtang!

Ordered Doncheongtang Shio Ramen and Tonkotsu Ramen.

I had shio ramen first and it was unusual that the ramen bowl had no base and they served it to me after saying it was hot.

When I took my first bite of the soup, I smelled something like butter, but after taking two or three more bites, it didn't come out lol. I wonder if my nose is acting weird today....
After that, I liked that the pork flavor was more subtle than I expected, and as I ate it more and more, it melted into the green onion soup, and my nose got used to it, so I started to focus on the taste rather than the smell.
Maybe that's why I liked the clean salty taste.

Menma complied with it without any inconveniences.
The char siu had a good fiery aroma without any unpleasant odour. It was quite thick and had a nice chewy texture.
The noodles were a little thicker than I expected and the cooking was just right for my taste.

And the second bowl, Tonkotsu Ramen!
I expected a thick but clean beef bone-like soup, but I was surprised that the pork bone flavor was stronger than I expected.
As with all rich tonkotsu, in my experience, this soup with a strong bone flavor goes very well with garlic. I added about a teaspoon and it suddenly turned into a top-quality pork soup.
I'm not sure because I didn't see the noodles side by side, but it seemed like the noodles were thinner than Shio's, but I'm not sure.
Everything else is the same

Personally, I liked Shio better, but the white soup was also delicious.

reviews.text:
I heard somewhere that a Japanese ramen restaurant made with beef fat had opened in Korea, so I marked it on the map and decided to visit because it was nearby.

Ordered Jiro Ramen and Shirunashi (all with added toppings, shoyu for both)

I already ate one bowl, so at first I only ordered soup with the intention of only eating one bowl.
As soon as I received it, a lot of question marks appeared in my head, and it was very far from the Jiro Ramen visual I knew.
No matter how much I ordered beef, this is all it consists of, sea burra, bean sprouts, and noodles without a single piece of chashu....??
I wonder why the composition is so poor...
But the taste is another story, so I tried the soup.
The taste is light without any three-dimensional effect, and other than the taste of soy sauce, there is no noticeable taste or scent.
The bean sprouts had a greenish smell and the seabura felt greasy, probably because it wasn't seasoned well, so I just mixed it all with the soup and ate it together, and now I could smell a hint of beef fat, as fragrant as brisket.
The garlic particles were thick and very spicy when chewed, and the noodles were okay.

However, even though this is my second bowl, the amount of jiro here is so small that I feel like one more bowl would be enough, so I tried 3 bowls for the first time in my life.

Additional order of shoyu sirunashi (I mixed the shirunashi and took a bite and took a picture)

When I mixed it and tried it, I thought it was saltier and more savory than the soup, so it tasted closer to what I was used to.
However, because of that, the beef fat flavor, which is the specialty of this place, was less strong, so I felt like I had to order Seaburra size M or larger. Other factors were not much different.

My portion size is average for an adult, and if I eat egg ramen + kimchi + rice, I'm full.
For example, with Jiro Ramen, 566 200g of regular noodles were left over, and at Ryujin, if you ate all the regular noodles, you would eat them all and feel very full.
But here, for the same price, the taste is lower and the quantity is less than half...

conclusion
Looking at the history, Jiro Ramen is synonymous with good value for money and generous portions of ramen, but for 13,000 won, it serves an amount that would not fill even an elementary school student, and it is the first time in my life that I have ever seen a ramen restaurant where you have to pay for extra chashu.
Also, what if it tastes amazingly good?
Other than the taste, the lighting was too dark and the chair couldn't be pulled all the way up, making it uncomfortable. I think there should be at least one Korean employee who can speak basic Korean, but the owner is alone and speaks only Japanese.
Taste, service, cost-effectiveness... I don't understand what kind of thinking and preparation went into opening a store in Korea.

Mapo Restaurant

This is a place that focuses on abura soba, and rather than a menu, the ‘versions’ of abura soba itself are diverse.
Based on the basic abura soba, there are different versions available, including curry, crab (kani), white, niboshi, and mackerel.

What I ate this time was the crab (kani) version. There are two crab stew cookies on top, which looks cute and actually tastes quite clearly of crab. It's natural and not forced, so it captures the unique greasiness of abura soba well. In general, rather than the heavy style of soy sauce and oil that Japanese men might like, the abura soba is rich and creamy, making it easy to eat.

You cannot add noodles, but you can add rice for free after the meal, and char siu is also provided. It's quite fun to finish by adding rice to the remaining sauce and mixing hot sauce, pepper, and mayonnaise.
The food came out very quickly, so there was a good rotation, and there was no wait when I visited at 4pm on a Saturday. Next time, I want to try a version other than Kani again.

Niboshi Aburasoba (extra spicy)

There weren't many people, so the food came out quickly, and the colors were so pretty that my expectations rose.
At first, as written in the instructions, I mixed it without the raw egg and took a bite. It felt like a very luxurious and refined snack food.
The salinity was between normal and salty according to newbies' standards, so I wanted it to be saltier, but as I ate it, the taste was well balanced, so halfway through I thought, "It's spicy, so this taste isn't that bad."
And among the toppings, I liked the chashu and menma the best, and when I mixed the raw egg in the middle, the taste became more rounded and I suddenly had a desire for customization.
I ate it one by one in the order it was placed, and it all went well together (pepper > vinegar > mayonnaise > hot sauce).

In conclusion, I think it would be better if there were more options, such as salt level selection or the Mania version menu that was sold out today.
It was delicious! I will visit again later

I came late and couldn't try one bite, but I think I'll try again. They say it is extremely well-ripened, chewy, sweet, and delicious. As I sat at the table, my mouth was watering as I watched the staff preparing the dishes across the semi-open kitchen.

I joined in the middle and received 32,000 won of Geumgetang, which looked amazing. Although they are only called golden crabs, I have seen at least 6 of them with my own eyes. There wasn't a lot of meat on the crab shells, but the legs had a pretty good yield. It was 70-80% full. Considering the amount of crab alone, the crab stew was worth 100,000 won.

And this restaurant's Hanayagu Junmai (45,000 won) is highly recommended. I don't drink sake very often, but the taste was very rich, probably because the "wine yeast" was alive. Looking at the ingredient name, does it say rice + yeast? It has a familiar MakgeolX taste, but would you say it tastes completely luxurious? The amount, 900mL, was enough for three people to drink.

There was so much gold crab stew that I asked for it to be packaged. Even though there was only half left, they kindly packaged it well. I'll have to go back next time to eat the sashimi I couldn't eat. The atmosphere is classy and comfortable. Almost all tables seat two, so it's good for two people. reviews.author: Chanwook Lee
reviews.text:
As Beomhongdae is a commercial area with a strong ramen core fan base, there are many prominent ramen restaurants, and among them, this is one that has been in business for over 20 years. As you can guess from the name, they serve Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen.

Therefore, although the main dish is tonkotsu, it is also famous for its late-night limited menu, chadoldanmyeon, served only after 10 p.m. Since I don't have time to stop by this neighborhood late at night, I don't always get to taste it, but when I got the chance, I found it.

It was past 10:30 p.m., but there was a wait, so I entered after waiting for about ten minutes. As it is a college town, there were young couples in front and back, and the flashy sound of a wok could be heard clearly from outside, further heating up the atmosphere.

The marbled noodles came out sooner than expected and were generous, 1.5 times the size of regular ramen. Because it was stir-fried in a wok, a thick layer of smoke rose, and the soup, with red pepper flakes floating in it, was intense.

There was quite a bit of brisket, but there was more cabbage and there was also zucchini in between. The soup was thick and thick, so it sharply scratched my throat, and the overall impression was a hybrid of stew and jjambbong.

The sweetness I was concerned about due to the cabbage was surprisingly not strong as it was undercooked to the point where it was crunchy. The noodles didn't spread, but they were soaked in a lot of broth and were gently chopped, which seemed to slightly neutralize the spiciness.

As I ate it, a heavy feeling of fat rose up, so I added a clove of crushed garlic and the soup became much less burdensome. It wasn't awkward to eat it like soup, so even though I couldn't finish it, I was able to eat all the ingredients.

I ate it as a late dinner rather than a late-night snack, so it felt a bit spicy and maniacal, but when I think of tonkotsu, it wasn't that intense. If it's a cold day, the taste will shine even more, and you can make a reservation for stomach relief the next day.

Kanda Soba's position feels like a ramen restaurant that might be popular with light fans rather than ramen lovers.
So, for those who are afraid of strong saltiness, you can try the Jiro here and gradually move on. The nuance of the taste is similar, but the taste is extremely mild.

Today, I was home alone, and I was feeling hungry in the evening, so I was thinking about what to eat. If I couldn't stop by Scent Grill Barbecue yesterday, I decided to stop by Teppan Tamago, which I was planning to stop by instead, and try Neapolitan spaghetti.

I like Neapolitan spaghetti cooked with ketchup, but Seo-gyeongsa, a coffee bar in Hapjeong where I could taste unique Neapolitan spaghetti, removed Neapolitan spaghetti from the menu the next day after I tried it, perhaps to focus only on the coffee, and Yangsongi Restaurant in Sinsu-dong seems to have added Neapolitan spaghetti to its menu again these days, but in any case, I prefer Neapolitan spaghetti or hamburger steak over the omurice at that store. It was better, but perhaps because of the influx of customers after their omurice was introduced on TV, they only served omurice to simplify the menu, so I wondered where I could go to try Neapolitan spaghetti.

It's not easy to find a store that serves Neapolitan spaghetti, and I don't want to go to a store that only sells the so-called Instagram-like taste but is expensive, so when I get the chance, I search for a store that serves my type of Neapolitan spaghetti. I found out that I can taste Neapolitan spaghetti at Teppan Tamago, which has an izakaya-like feel where okonomiyaki is the main menu, and I also heard that somewhere a Japanese person cooks it. I thought I'd seen it before, so it seemed like it was a restaurant with a Japanese-style pasta menu, so I decided to visit it with my family. The Neapolitan spaghetti was soggy, and most of the menu was crap, so I saved it in I want to go, wondering if it was at least better than the nameless pasta in Gangnam Station, which made me angry.

Originally, I was going to stop by Battle Tteokbokki first, but Teppan Tamago is an izakaya-style restaurant, so I wasn't going to drink and I was stopping by for dinner, so I thought it would be better to stop by early in the evening when there wouldn't be many customers, so I decided to stop by first.

The store was located in a building next to the Patagonia store, and when I entered the store, it felt a bit acrid because the food was cooked on an iron plate and the ventilation was not good, and the store did not feel very clean. Since I was alone, I was told to sit at the bar table in front of the iron plate, and without even looking at the menu, I asked for Neapolitan spaghetti.

First, they gave me a plate and a cutting tool for eating pickled radish and okonomiyaki, so I ate niapolitan spaghetti. Why did they give me something like this?

Okonomiyaki, probably ordered by other customers, was being cooked on the iron plate, and listening to the conversation between the employees, the man cooking it seemed like a Korean who could speak Japanese, and the two women, whether it was a female clerk or the owner, seemed Japanese.

I think the Neapolitan spaghetti I ordered needs to be cooked in a pan, but the male chef was frying the thin pork belly and garlic that go on top of the okonomiyaki on an iron plate, so I thought I would have to wait a little longer for my order. But he sprinkled cooked spaghetti noodles and ketchup that go well with Neapolitan spaghetti on top of the pork belly and garlic that he had just fried and started frying them again, so I thought that was the Neapolitan spaghetti I ordered. There is no standard Neapolitan spaghetti, but this is the first time I've seen a type that uses thin pork belly instead of the usual Vienna sausages, so I'm curious what it would taste like.

After it was cooked, Parmesan cheese powder was sprinkled on top of the Neapolitan spaghetti, a fried egg was placed on top, green onion powder was sprinkled on top, and it was placed on a plate on an iron plate and placed in front of it. It was a bit unfamiliar that it was cooked on an iron plate rather than a common frying pan, which I had expected from a restaurant that serves food cooked on an iron plate, and the way it was served was not common and felt like an izakaya, so I was a little confused, and the volume felt like a snack rather than a meal, and I was a little disappointed. I feel it.

Overall, the seasoning wasn't too strong, so it was easy to eat without feeling burdened.

reviews.author: Productive Minho
reviews.text:
This is a restaurant that mainly serves tonkotsu ramen and tantanmen, and I ordered Kyokai tonkotsu and bomb ramen (tantan). Compared to other ramen restaurants, this place has a saltier, richer flavor and richer oil. Hosomen, a thin noodle, is used. If you are trying ramen for the first time, it may be irritating and greasy. Garlic is an important topping for the ramen here.

The Kyokai Tonkotsu Ramen here was a tonkotsu base mixed with sababushi (smoked blue fish). The combination of pork broth and dried fish can have a strong fishy smell, but it wasn't bad. Rather than the savory taste of seafood that is characteristic of Kyokai, the sababushi-like scent of anchovies seemed to be particularly strong.

I ordered bomb ramen level 2 and it was a little spicier than Shin Ramen. It's called Sichuan-style Dantanmen with Jiro's special stir-fried seasoning, and since it's a ramen restaurant, they use sea burra, so the taste of tonkotsu is also important in this Dantanmen. For my taste, I liked Bomb Ramen better than Kyokai. The chashu is soft but has a strong soy sauce taste.

reviews.author: Seungwook Jeong
reviews.text:
For the representative menu item, Jiou Ramen, you can choose whether the broth is thick or not thick. If you eat it thick, it will taste greasy instead of thick.
When I tried it thickly, it didn't feel greasy or smell bad.
The taste was not different from regular tonkotsu ramen and was just edible, but I saw a sign telling me to add garlic when paying, but I would have tried it that way if it had been at every table, so it was disappointing.
The noodles come out moderately stiff. Char siu, soft boiled.
The chashu rice bowl was cold and not very good. Maybe it was because it was cold, but it only tasted salty. It felt like I received a piece of bread.
Gyoza is just gyoza
Overall, soso

reviews.author: Kihyun Kwon
reviews.text:
Tsukemen, the representative menu item, had really thick and chewy noodles with a good texture, and the broth for dipping it was thick but not overpowering and had a well-balanced taste. It wasn't greasy so I didn't have to worry about finishing it.

The portion was generous enough for an adult male, and I was impressed by the fact that the noodles maintained their flavor even when they cooled down. There is also a spicy menu, but it is at a level that anyone can enjoy, rather than being spicy.

The store is not large, so there may be a wait during peak times, but turnover is quick.
Recommended if you want to eat authentic tsukemen neatly in Hongdae!

reviews.author: PY_Z
reviews.text:
I visited on a very cold day. It's located in an alley across from Hongmungwan, the main gate of Hongik University, so you have to walk quite a bit if you walk from the subway. It's on the first floor, so it's not difficult to find.
I went to avoid the main meal time and was able to enter without waiting. After ordering at the kiosk and sitting down, the food comes out and I ordered Tsukeman. You can choose the amount of noodles between 200 and 300 grams, and if you order 300, you don't have to pay extra.

When the food came out, I was surprised because the dipping sauce was so clear and thin. I think I was confused because it was a different style from what I was used to eating in Japan.
Usually, I've only tried the thicker style of darae sauce.

The noodles were ordered at 300, so the quantity was large. It was written that the noodles were homemade, and they seemed to be very springy and thin udon noodles, but the texture was good.
The meat in the chashu and sauce was too dry and not that good.

It was my first time trying Tsukeman style, and the taste itself was good so I enjoyed it.
However, it tastes a bit too sour.

reviews.author: Alex Mun
reviews.text:
Even if you add 100g to the basic 300g tsukemen, it is good for an adult man to eat alone.
Tsukemen's sauce is made up of pork broth and a lot of oil, but it's not thick, so it's a light sauce, but it has a lot of oil and actually contains four chunks of pork fat. Even if you order double karaage, it is not spicy. Anseongtangmyeon is not even spicy. The noodles are chewy, and the char siu is nothing special, just three thin layers. The portion of Soyu Ramen Karai was large and impressive. There are a variety of ingredients for the thin noodles, but the pepper taste and aroma are too strong, perhaps because too much pepper was added. However, it is good value for money, and Yaki Gyoza is just a dumpling that tastes like flour and is not very filling.
I don't think I'll come back again as I prefer the rich and thick taste of tsukemen. However, it doesn't mean it's tasteless or bad, it just seems to be a matter of taste.

reviews.text: This is actually not a curry restaurant, but a Japanese-style hayashi donburi (a dish made with minced beef on rice). I ordered mushroom hayashi rice bowl and grilled vegetables and it was really delicious! The main dish had 3-4 different types of mushrooms and the vegetables included eggplant and shishito peppers, all grilled to perfection. I've tried Hayashi Donburi at other places, but I didn't really know what it tasted like until I heard owner Ho explain it. The Hayashi sauce here was light but rich and flavorful. Overall, it was a really satisfying meal, and it was a refreshing change from Korean food, which can feel heavy due to its strong taste.

reviews.author: ethan ghymn
reviews.text:
On my way near Hapjeong Station, I heard from an acquaintance that nearby Kami Udon's Wakame Udon was good, and I wasn't necessarily drawn to Wakame Udon with seaweed, but since I ate a croissant at home in the morning, I wanted to eat something other than bread, so I decided to stop by Star Burger, which I wanted to visit in this neighborhood, next time and headed to Kami Udon.

It wasn't long before I arrived in front of the store, and since it was lunch time, I thought the waiting line would be long because it was so popular, but it was dark and it felt scary for a moment.

As I got closer, it said it was closed on Mondays. Wow..

I had no choice but to go to Star Burger where I originally wanted to go. As expected, we're almost there, but it's still intense. Wow... Monday was a regular holiday in this house too.

Nearby, I remembered Dangin-dong Noodle Factory, which I saved because the mung bean pancake I saw in Pyeongnaengjaengi's review looked delicious and I wanted to go there, so I looked it up on Naver Maps and found that this place is also closed on Mondays.

There are the most houses in this neighborhood that I have saved in I Want to Go, but right now I can't see any houses I want to go to that I haven't been to, so I'm thinking of nearby Shinyatenya.

I've seen it several times in passing, and I remember going into Yeoksam Renaissance Store last weekend and just leaving, so I decided to stop by.

I don't really like chain stores, but I decided to go in front and check out the atmosphere. It was a little before 12 o'clock, and I saw two male customers ordering at the kiosk. I went inside the store and looked at the menu, and the Ebitendon with 4 shrimp caught my eye. It wasn't just Ebitendon, but it said "Daebitendon", so I was drawn to it.

The tendon at Hyeongje Donburi in Magok-dong, Gangseo-gu, which I recently visited after reading Rachel's review, was not that special. It had the same feel as the tendon of the old Hongdae donburi when it was popular. However, I was dissatisfied with the shrimp tempura at tendon restaurants these days because it felt like it was getting smaller and smaller, but the shrimp tempura was quite large, so I was satisfied with it. However, it was written as a large ebi tendon, so I decided to try it out and ordered at the kiosk.

As soon as you enter the store, there is a kitchen on the left. There is a chef who frys tempura, and a younger male employee who seems to be an assistant is in charge of setting up and serving the food. There was a Datchi seat right in front of the kitchen, and there were table seats inside the store. I was guided and sat at the Datchi seat.

As I sat in the Dodge seat and looked around the store, I felt like the owner and chef had put some effort into the atmosphere as it wasn't run by the owner himself, or it felt like a chain store and the store didn't have a very clean atmosphere.

When I entered the store, I noticed that vegetables were fried in advance, but fortunately, the shrimp were fried right after ordering.

Perhaps because it was lunch time, customers kept coming in, but the owner/chef didn't seem very happy about the customers coming in. When I asked if I should wait when a customer ordered, he answered that the food would be prepared according to the order, so you would have to wait to eat it, but I secretly felt like he wanted me to just go back.

The menu said that the special sauce had a thick consistency, but in Korea, people don't like strong flavors, so I thought it would come out with just a little bit of sauce, so I asked for a little more sauce in advance.

The meals of the first two male guests were served first, followed by the large ebi tendon that I ordered. The miso soup that came with it was a common taste, nothing special.

When I looked at Daebi Tendon, it was good that it was served in a relatively large bowl like the Tendon at Hyeongje Donburi that I visited last time, and that it was not as small as the bowls at Ichizen or other popular Tendon restaurants these days. As written on the menu, the shrimp tempura is relatively large in size, so I like it more than the tendon restaurants that serve shrimp tempura the size of a few fingers. In addition, as expected, there are perilla leaves and crown crown fries that are not too small in size.

I eat rice with sauce sprinkled on it with chopsticks. The sauce tastes sweet and salty, so it's not bad. I asked for a little more sauce earlier, but I'm not sure if they forgot or if they sprinkled a little too much to make it better, but the taste was strong enough, so I sat down and asked for a little more sauce.

I received tendon with a little more sauce and tried the shrimp tempura this time. The crispy, crumbly batter was not bad and the size was quite large. However, it is a bit disappointing that the fried perilla leaves and crown crown were a bit harder and not warm enough, probably because they were fried in advance.

By the time I finished eating two shrimp tempura, I didn't have enough rice, so I asked for more rice and sauce. I ate it deliciously until the end and woke up.

I didn't like chain stores in general, so I was reluctant to visit, and in fact, I didn't like the feel of the store or the staff because it felt like a chain store, but the well-fried Ebitendon with 4 relatively large shrimp was satisfactory for the price, so I felt it was a better visit than waiting in a long line at some strangely popular Tendon specialty stores, even though they weren't particularly delicious or used real ingredients. However, since it has the atmosphere of a chain restaurant, I am not sure if I will visit again.

reviews.author: korean
reviews.text:
I stopped by without thinking, but it is no exaggeration to say that it was the most delicious ramen I have ever had in Hongdae. I had Tsugemen & Yuzu Tsuyu Ramen, and the Yuzu Tsuyu Ramen was truly amazing. The soup was refreshing, sweet, yet salty, and not overpowering. The meat was very delicious, and even though it was pork, it had a slightly seasoned rib-like feel to it, which was impressive. Although there was a little bit of blood, as someone who likes the meat rare, it felt soft and good.

Tsugemen is eaten dipped in red sauce, and is a bit different from the Japanese style we commonly know. Rather, the sweet and sour sauce was impressive enough to remind me of Paldo bibim noodles, and it tasted perfect to eat on a hot summer day. Both menus were impressive, but personally, Tsuyu Ramen was much more memorable.

The interior of the store may have been a bar in the past, but it still had a bit of that atmosphere, and the seating was a bit unusual as many people sat together at large tables, but it wasn't uncomfortable. The staff were very friendly and explained the food in detail, so I was satisfied with the overall service. As a side dish, instead of fried chicken or Japanese side dishes, they served green onion kimchi, which surprisingly went well together, making it a perfect combination for Korean tastes.

To sum it up, it is a ramen restaurant that no Korean can dislike, and it was a place I would definitely want to come back to again. However, I am not sure if this is a global taste.

reviews.author: JS Park
reviews.text:
This is a shio ramen restaurant in Hongdae.
The location is closer to Sangsu Station.
Yuzushio ramen with yuzu is the main product.
I think they used chicken broth, and it was very well made, clean and flavorful.
The noodles are made of three noodles, and you can clearly feel the subtle citron scent.
Uniquely, the noodles and broth are unlimited refills, so you can request them multiple times.
I refilled it 3 times and was satisfied.
Tsukemen is not a typical thick sauce, but a spicy sauce with yuzu in it, and people seem to have mixed opinions about this.
If you refill the broth after eating all the noodles and make soup, it is surprisingly delicious.
I was satisfied with the ramen because it was very well made.

Korean restaurant serving beef as the main dish
#Semo Restaurant

They sell a unique menu called boiled beef stew.

Recommended menu: Boiled beef stew, raw meat

The boiled pork casserole that melts in a soup like rib soup is excellent as a side dish with drinks.

What really surprised me here was the raw meat.

The raw meat served in a style similar to sashimi had the texture of raw meat from a high-end beef restaurant.

The slightly pleasant stickiness and rich flavor keep me reaching for it.

Although it is Sangsu, the atmosphere is quiet and it is a good place for conversation.
